Trying to Conceive

Varicocele before conception: observation, repair and fertility

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A varicocele does not automatically prevent pregnancy or require treatment before you try. Some people conceive without repair; others benefit from a fertility assessment and selected treatment. The useful question is how the confirmed finding fits with symptoms, semen results, both partners’ reproductive health and the time available: not whether every enlarged vein should be operated on.

What a varicocele is

A varicocele is enlargement of the network of veins that drains blood from a testicle, called the pampiniform plexus. Blood can pool rather than flow away efficiently. The exact cause is not always clear; vein valves and the route of the blood vessels can contribute. It is a vein problem around the testicle, not a blockage of the sperm-carrying tube.

It often develops around puberty and is more common on the left, although it can affect the right or both sides. It is found in people with and without fertility difficulties. Population estimates vary; neither a percentage nor the appearance of the veins tells you whether you personally can conceive. It is often uncomplicated, but calling every varicocele harmless would overlook pain, testicular growth changes or relevant fertility findings.

Symptoms need a confirmed diagnosis

Many people notice no symptoms. Others have a dull ache or heaviness, especially after standing or later in the day, that may ease when lying down. Larger veins may look or feel like a soft cluster above the testicle. An affected testicle can be smaller. None of these findings confirms the diagnosis at home or proves the veins caused a fertility problem.

Have new swelling, a lump, a change in size or persistent discomfort examined. Sudden severe testicular pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain continuing at rest needs emergency care immediately. Do not assume it is your known varicocele: torsion and other urgent conditions can occur separately. Arrange safe transport instead of driving yourself in an emergency.

What examination and ultrasound can show

A clinician examines the scrotum and both testicles, usually standing and lying down. They may ask you to bear down briefly while holding a breath (the Valsalva manoeuvre) to make veins easier to assess. You can ask for an explanation and appropriate privacy. Repeatedly squeezing the area or using a photograph to grade it is not a substitute for examination.

A clinical varicocele is one the clinician can feel; a subclinical one is found only on imaging. Doppler ultrasound can clarify an uncertain examination, another suspected cause or a persistent finding after treatment. An ultrasound report alone is not a reason to repair nonpalpable veins for fertility. A new, large or non-reducing finding may need additional assessment; a right-sided finding does not automatically mean cancer or require the same scan for everyone.

Semen testing answers a different question

Semen analysis assesses sperm concentration and number, movement and shape. Normal-looking semen, comfortable ejaculation or a visible varicocele cannot tell you those results. Follow the laboratory’s collection instructions and report an incomplete sample, recent fever and medicines. An abnormal result can coexist with a varicocele without proving that the veins are its only cause.

There is no universal requirement for at least three tests. An abnormal result commonly needs confirmation, with timing chosen for the clinical situation. WHO’s 2025 initial-assessment guidance suggests repeating outside-range results after at least 11 weeks, while other pathways differ. Very low or absent sperm and other concerning findings warrant timely specialist discussion rather than waiting to complete a fixed series. A result within reference ranges is not a guarantee of pregnancy.

Trying naturally and assessing both partners

Natural conception can still happen with a varicocele, including in some people with abnormal semen results. A confirmed, comfortable varicocele is not by itself a reason to stop trying while an agreed evaluation proceeds. The chance depends on the full semen pattern, ovulation, tubes, age and other circumstances; no single vein grade supplies a reliable personal pregnancy percentage.

Arrange assessment of both partners together. Common referral advice is after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse if the egg-producing partner is under 35, or 6 months at 35 or older; local pathways vary. Over 40, or with known or suspected fertility problems, seek advice sooner. Do not delay one partner’s evaluation while the other repeats tests or waits for a procedure.

When observation is reasonable

Observation may be appropriate when a confirmed varicocele causes no important symptoms and there is no relevant testicular or fertility impairment. Routine repair to improve fertility is generally not recommended for an ultrasound-only varicocele or normal semen results. If a couple still has unexplained infertility despite apparently normal results, the specialist should review the whole situation rather than assume there is nothing to investigate.

Follow-up should match symptoms, testicular findings and reproductive plans. Persistent pain and impaired testicular growth can justify a separate treatment discussion, especially in adolescents, even when conception is not the immediate goal. Most adolescents do not need preventive surgery simply because a varicocele exists. Supportive underwear and suitable pain relief may help a diagnosed mild ache; they must not delay assessment of new or acute pain.

When repair may help: and what remains uncertain

Current specialist guidance supports considering repair for selected people trying to conceive who have a palpable varicocele, infertility and abnormal semen parameters. It may improve semen findings and the chance of pregnancy. The blanket idea that repair never improves pregnancy outcomes is therefore not a sound rule. Equally, improvement is not guaranteed, and a better semen result is not the same as a live birth.

WHO’s 2025 recommendation is conditional and identifies uncertainty about live-birth benefit; its recommendation concerns clinical varicocele in infertile couples not undergoing assisted reproduction. With no sperm in semen, or proposed repair before sperm retrieval or IVF/ICSI, the evidence and alternatives need specialist discussion. Selected cases involving high sperm DNA fragmentation or unsuccessful fertility treatment may be considered, but these are not reasons for everyone to order extra tests or seek surgery.

Compare procedures and their risks

Surgery closes selected enlarged veins so blood drains through other routes. Microsurgery uses magnification to identify veins while protecting arteries and lymphatic vessels; other surgical approaches also exist. Embolisation uses an image-guided catheter to block affected veins, often with local anaesthetic. Neither treatment removes the testicle. Expertise, anatomy, previous treatment, preferences and access help determine the choice.

Possible harms include bleeding or bruising, infection, persistent or recurrent veins and continuing or altered pain. Surgery can injure a testicular artery and, rarely, harm or shrink the testicle; damage to lymphatic drainage can cause a hydrocele, which is fluid around the testicle, not inside it. Embolisation can involve contrast allergy, vein injury or failure to complete the treatment. Ask about the specific technique’s risks and the operator’s experience; neither approach guarantees symptom relief or pregnancy.

Plan recovery and the time to reassessment

Physical recovery and fertility improvement run on different timelines. Follow the treating team’s instructions about wounds, activity, pain medicine and when sex can resume; there is no single safe date for every procedure. Follow-up semen testing and any change in conception chances take longer than the skin puncture or incision takes to heal, often requiring several months of assessment.

Discuss that delay before choosing treatment, particularly when the other partner’s age, ovarian reserve or another problem makes time important. Assisted conception, such as IVF with or without ICSI, may be an alternative or part of the plan. Agree when to review results, what happens if they do not improve and how to respond to recurrence. New severe pain, fever or worsening postoperative swelling needs prompt advice from the treating service or emergency care when severe.

Health measures support care; they do not close the veins

Regular activity, a sustainable balanced diet, smoking cessation and reducing heavy alcohol use support general and reproductive health. Review avoidable repeated heat and occupational chemical exposure with appropriate protection. These steps do not prove that a varicocele will disappear or that pregnancy will follow. Do not blame yourself for the finding or postpone a needed assessment while trying to perfect your habits.

Bring prescription medicines, supplements and any testosterone or anabolic steroid use to the appointment. Do not stop prescribed treatment on your own; external testosterone can suppress sperm production rather than improve fertility. Fertility supplements and antioxidants have uncertain benefits and are not a substitute for an individual plan. Record symptoms, results and both partners’ priorities so the decision about observation, repair or assisted conception is clear.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Confirm the diagnosis and arrange semen assessment and review of both partners when indicated.

Ask how observation, repair or assisted conception fits your findings, risks and reproductive timetable.

Agree follow-up and urgent-symptom instructions; do not replace assessment with home remedies or supplements.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can organise symptom notes, semen reports, medicines, appointments and questions for both partners. It cannot diagnose or grade a varicocele, interpret a report as a fertility guarantee, choose a procedure or predict a pregnancy.

When to seek help

Sudden severe testicular pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain continuing at rest needs emergency care. New lumps, swelling or persistent changes need examination even with a previous varicocele diagnosis. Do not drive yourself in an emergency or delay care for home comfort measures.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A varicocele can coexist with normal fertility; the diagnosis is not an automatic instruction for surgery.
  • Clinical examination and the whole semen assessment matter more than an ultrasound label alone.
  • Selected repair may improve pregnancy chances, with uncertainty and no guaranteed live birth.
  • Compare observation, procedure risks and treatment delays in the context of both partners.
  • New or severe testicular symptoms need assessment even if a varicocele was diagnosed before.

Frequently asked questions

What exactly is a varicocele?

It is enlarged veins in the drainage network around a testicle. It is usually left-sided, can occur on either or both sides and is different from a blocked sperm duct. A clinician should confirm the diagnosis.

What signs can it cause?

Often none. A dull standing ache, heaviness, visible or palpable veins or a smaller affected testicle can occur. New lumps or changes need assessment; sudden severe pain, pain with sickness or abdominal pain, or pain at rest is an emergency.

Does it necessarily damage sperm?

No. Some people have normal semen and conceive without repair; others have impaired findings. Semen testing and the wider assessment help establish what matters. Neither a varicocele nor one abnormal sample proves the whole cause, and three tests are not universally required.

Must it be treated before trying for pregnancy?

Not automatically. Observation can be appropriate, while selected palpable varicoceles with infertility and abnormal semen may benefit from repair. Decide with a specialist using symptoms, results, both partners’ health and time; neither mandatory surgery nor a blanket no-benefit claim is accurate.

Does an ultrasound-only finding need surgery?

Repair is not routinely recommended for fertility when the veins cannot be felt on examination and are found only on imaging. A scan may still be useful to clarify other findings; the whole clinical assessment matters.

What if semen results are normal?

Routine fertility-directed repair is generally not recommended. Symptoms, testicular growth and an ongoing unexplained fertility problem may still need review. A normal result is not a guarantee of conception or a reason to ignore either partner’s assessment.

Can repair guarantee a baby or replace IVF?

No. It may improve findings or pregnancy chances in selected cases, but live-birth evidence and individual outcomes remain uncertain. The choice between waiting, repair and assisted conception depends on both partners and the time available; no-sperm findings need a specialist plan.

How soon can we try after a procedure?

Ask the surgeon or radiologist when sex and usual activity can safely resume. That recovery timetable differs from the months that may be needed to reassess semen and fertility. Agree a review date and next steps rather than relying on a universal deadline.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
